title: like, as if
subtitle: You look like you haven't slept
summary: Learn to use like, as if and as though to say how somebody or something looks, sounds, feels or behaves.

lesson.heading: look / sound / feel + like or as if
lesson.text: We use **like** or **as if** to say how somebody or something looks, sounds or feels. Both are followed by a subject and a verb.

examples.text: That house looks **like it's going to fall down**.
examples.note: or ... looks as if it's going to fall down

examples.text: Amy sounded **as if she had a cold**, didn't she?
examples.note: or Amy sounded like she had a cold

examples.text: I've just had a holiday, but I feel very tired. I don't feel **as if I've had a holiday**.
examples.note: or I don't feel like I've had a holiday

lesson.note: You can also use as though: I don't feel as though I've had a holiday.

lesson.heading: look + adjective or look like + subject + verb

right.label: look like / as if + subject + verb
examples: You look **as if you haven't slept**.

lesson.heading: It looks like ... / It sounds like ...
lesson.text: We often start with **it looks like ...** or **it sounds like ...** to say what we think is happening, from what we can see or hear. **as if** and **as though** are also possible.

examples.text: Sarah is very late. **It looks like she isn't coming.**
examples.note: or It looks as if she isn't coming

examples.text: **It looked like it was going to rain**, so we took an umbrella.
The noise is very loud next door. **It sounds like they're having a party.**
examples.note: or It sounds as though they're having a party

lesson.heading: With other verbs
lesson.text: You can use **like / as if / as though** with other verbs too, to say how somebody does something.

examples.text: He ran **like he was running for his life**.
After the interruption, the speaker went on talking **as if nothing had happened**.
When I told them my plan, they looked at me **as though I was mad**.

lesson.heading: as if + past for something unreal
lesson.text: After **as if** we sometimes use the past when we are talking about the present. The meaning is not past: we use the past because the idea is not real. We do not normally use *like* in this way.

examples.text: I don't like him. He talks **as if he knew everything**.
She's always asking me to do things for her - **as if I didn't have enough to do already**.
examples.note: I have enough to do already

examples.text: Joe's only 40. Why do you talk about him **as if he was an old man**?

lesson.heading: as if he were ...
lesson.text: When you use the past in this way, you can use **were** instead of *was*. Both are correct.

examples.text: Why do you talk about him **as if he were an old man**?
They treat me **as if I were their own son**.
examples.note: or ... as if I was their own son

lesson.text: After *look/sound/feel*, use an adjective on its own (You look tired) but *like / as if* before a subject and verb (You look as if you're tired).

exercises.prompt: You meet Bill. He has a black eye and blood on his face. You say to him: You ___ in a fight.
exercises.explanation: look like + subject + verb describes how somebody looks.

exercises.prompt: Claire comes into the room and looks absolutely terrified. You say: What's the matter? You ___ a ghost.
answers: look as if you have seen
exercises.explanation: as if + subject + verb: you look as if you've seen a ghost.

exercises.prompt: You have just run one kilometre, but you are exhausted. You say: I ___ a marathon.
exercises.explanation: feel like + subject + verb says how something feels to you.

exercises.prompt: Joe is on holiday. He phones you and sounds happy. You say to him: You ___ a good time.
answers: sound as if you are having
exercises.explanation: sound as if + subject + verb says how somebody sounds.

exercises.prompt: Match each situation with what you would say.

pairs.left: Sarah said she would be here an hour ago.
pairs.right: It looks like she isn't coming.

pairs.left: The sky is full of black clouds.
pairs.right: It looks like it's going to rain.

pairs.left: Two people are shouting at each other next door.
pairs.right: It sounds like they're having an argument.

pairs.left: You see an ambulance and two damaged cars at the roadside.
pairs.right: It looks like there's been an accident.

pairs.left: Dave isn't feeling well and tells you all about it.
pairs.right: It sounds like you should see a doctor.

exercises.prompt: You and a friend are looking for bananas in a supermarket, without success. What do you say?
options: It looks like they don't have any.
It looks they don't have any.
It looks like as if they don't have any.
exercises.explanation: It looks like + subject + verb. We never combine like and as if.

exercises.prompt: Mark looks very tired. He looks ___ a good rest.
exercises.explanation: as if + subject + verb describes the impression he gives.

exercises.prompt: Paul was extremely hungry and ate his dinner very quickly. He ate ___ for a week.
answers: as if he had not eaten
exercises.explanation: The idea is not real, so we go one tense back: as if he hadn't eaten.

exercises.prompt: I went into the office, but nobody spoke to me or looked at me. Everybody ignored me ___.
answers: as if I did not exist
exercises.explanation: The past after as if shows that the idea is not real - of course I exist.

exercises.statement: They treat me as if I were their own son.
exercises.explanation: Correct. After as if you can use were instead of was when the idea is not real.

exercises.prompt: I'm 20 years old, so please don't talk to me ___ a child.
exercises.explanation: For an unreal idea we use as if + past (as if I was/were), not like.

exercises.prompt: Andy is a terrible driver. Put the parts in order to describe how he drives.
exercises.answer: He drives as if he were the only driver on the road.
exercises.explanation: as if + past (were) because the idea is not real - other drivers do exist.
